look_here_first: ANNUAL BLUEGRASS — INTRODUCED, usually low cool-season annual. Recognize low soft green flowering tufts, often many small open triangular panicles and folded boat-prow leaf tips. The NEW macro really shows the boat tip, and the NEW four-view photo shows a membrane-like LIGULE at the blade/sheath junction. BOTH details are shared by other Poa: for species confirmation, document an intact rooted tuft (usually no persistent connected rhizomes) and a ripe spikelet of normally bisexual florets. The length of a photographed ligule or green head alone is NOT decisive.

best_field_traits: Cool-season generally annual; persistent biotypes can occur in managed moist turf.
Low flowering tuft with small spreading greenish seedheads; can flower under close mowing.
Young folded blades have prow-like boat-shaped tips; this is a genus clue NOT species-specific.
Ligule membranous around 0.5–3 mm according to Williamson County treatment; no auricles.
Spikelets commonly with bisexual florets; unlike separate-sex Texas bluegrass.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: True same-plant rooted annual tuft and basal tillers, including soil-contact roots (permitted collection only)
Whole low green mature panicle with a centimeter ruler and single spikelet without shaking off florets
Under 10–20×: one intact spikelet with outer glumes and bisexual floret features; lemma hair position and length, measured
One Poa leaf-tip macro and true membranous collar (already supplied via CC licensed references; still collect matched local voucher photo)
crew_field_check: Find the small low flowering tuft and whole open green panicle; compare the existing Harry Rose field photo.
See actual 30× photo of folded boat-PROW tip: same general character in both annual and Texas bluegrass; it is NOT a species shortcut.
See Stefan.lefnaer's source-photo composite: distinguish the actual thin pale membranous LIGULE from surrounding leaf sheath and blade; the white 10-mm photo bar isn't the ligule length.
Follow the same grass into a rooted base: annual P. annua usually forms small tillers and lacks Texas bluegrass-like persistent rhizomes, but some biotypes persist beyond a year.
Inspect ripe spikelets for bisexual florets and measured lemma keels; compare to dioecious Texas bluegrass and possible introduced P. pratensis. If not verified, leave Poa sp.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Contrast native P. arachnifera: perennial connected RHIZOMES and separate male/female flowering individuals; a pistillate female's ripe lemma bases produce dense long cobwebby hair tufts, while P. annua flowers generally bisexual and may have keel/marginal hairs but lacks the massive female web character. Do not guess sex or exact lemma hairs from landscape photos; compare P. pratensis and P. trivialis separately where common lawn grasses overlap.
not_reliable_alone: Boat-shaped grass leaf tip is a genus trait common to both Poa species
One very green or woolly head photographed at a distance, without sex/lemma macro
Ligule without the complete rooted specimen
Treating state native range as a Hays county voucher

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — SMALL GREEN PANICLE, THEN ROOTED BASE
field_id_short_tiles.short: Low cool-season introduced bluegrass; open triangular panicles, soft folded blades and boat-prow tips are useful clues, not species proof.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Follow ONE plant from its panicle to basal tillers. A small loose green panicle (Kew 1–12 cm; UT Austin local 7–9.5 cm) and hooded leaf tips suggest Poa, but P. arachnifera and lawn Poa share the tip. P. annua is usually annual and tufted, although some turf biotypes persist or root at nodes; absence of a visible rhizome in a landscape photograph proves nothing.
field_id_short_tiles.status: FIELD CUE VISIBLE — CONNECTED LOCAL ROOTED BASE NEEDED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · TRUE MEMBRANOUS LIGULE / COLLAR
field_id_short_tiles.short: Open the INNER blade–sheath junction: a pale unfringed membrane, often ~2–5 mm in Kew's treatment; local descriptions may be shorter.
field_id_short_tiles.details: The true ligule is a tissue flap, NOT the folded boat tip or a white portion of the sheath. Kew GrassBase describes an eciliate membranous ligule 2–5 mm; existing Williamson County treatment gives approximately 0.5–3 mm. The source-authenticated Stefan.lefnaer four-view collar photograph includes a genuine 10-mm bar but does not prove a precise measurement on a Hays plant. Poa arachnifera also has a membranous ligule; inspect reproductive characters.
field_id_short_tiles.status: REAL SOURCE COLLAR PHOTO — SAME-PLANT 1-MM MEASUREMENT NEEDED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · MATURE SPIKELETS / FLOWERING SEX
field_id_short_tiles.short: Many-flowered awnless spikelets: local Texas description ~3–5 mm with 2–6 florets; Kew's broader treatment ~3–10 mm and 3–10 fertile florets.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Measure an intact mature spikelet, excluding the stalk, before dissection. Each laterally compressed spikelet bears two basal glumes and multiple florets. UT Austin describes lower/intermediate florets generally bisexual, with upper florets sometimes pistillate or vestigial; DO NOT teach that every floret is invariably bisexual. Texas bluegrass is dioecious (male and female plants separate). Existing Harry Rose spikelet photographs do not independently show sex or separate organ boundaries.
field_id_short_tiles.status: PUBLISHED SEX/MEASUREMENTS — LOCAL DISSECTION STILL NEEDED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · LOWER / UPPER GLUME MEASUREMENTS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Lower glume ~1.4–3 mm, usually 1-veined; upper ~2–4 mm, usually 3-veined (Texas/Kew treatment ranges).
field_id_short_tiles.details: UT Austin's Central Texas description gives lower 1.4–2 mm and upper 2–2.5 mm; Kew GrassBase gives lower 1.5–3 mm (1 vein) and upper 2–4 mm (3 veins). Separate BOTH persistent glumes at the spikelet base and photograph front/back with a 1-mm scale before drawing any vein or glume arrow. The photographed overlapping green scales do not resolve which is which.
field_id_short_tiles.status: PUBLISHED ANATOMY — MEASURED SEPARATED GLUMES NEEDED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · FERTILE LEMMA / PALEA / AWN AND LOOK-ALIKES
field_id_short_tiles.short: Fertile lemma ~2.5–4 mm, usually 5-veined, often hairy along veins; NO lemma awn.
field_id_short_tiles.details: UT Austin gives the lowest lemma ~2.5–3.2 mm; Kew gives ~2.5–4 mm, five-veined and awnless. The palea sits inside the lemma, has two keels and may bear keel hairs. Compare native Texas bluegrass (P. arachnifera): connected perennial rhizomes and separate male/female flowering individuals; source-authenticated Harms female images show cobwebby basal lemma hairs, but this character must be viewed on real female florets. Introduced Kentucky bluegrass (P. pratensis) is also rhizomatous but has bisexual flowers; P. trivialis may be stoloniferous. Never use boat-tip, green color or web-like texture alone to name the species.
field_id_short_tiles.status: SOURCE ANATOMY + LOOK-ALIKES — DISSECTION/SEX STILL UNPROVEN
